posts.title: Discover Bintang's Spicy Sambal Chicken Inasal
posts.excerpt: Using our house Sambal Ulek sauce developed 30 years ago we are literally smashing our best selling Oak Smoked Chicken Inasal.

image.alt: Sambal chicken inasal with red onion, chilli and coriander

runs.text: Savour the Uniqueness of Bintang's Latest Menu Addition

At Bintang, we're thrilled to introduce a sensational new dish crafted from the original recipe of our esteemed owner, Omar Shah: Bintang's Sambal Inasal. This unique creation features our signature Oak Smoked Chicken Inasal, which undergoes a remarkable transformation - it's smashed! This method is not just for show; it tenderises the chicken, creating crevices that allow our special sambal sauce to permeate every bite.
What Makes Our Sambal Sauce Exceptional?

Our sambal sauce is inspired by the traditional Indonesian "Sambal Ulek (Oelek)," known for its robust spiciness and vibrant, fresh flavours. However, Bintang's version elevates this with a unique twist, incorporating fiery Naga chilies—akin to Scotch Bonnets chilli but with a fruity zest—along with copious amounts of garlic, ginger, and the exotic sweetness of mangosteen, our secret ingredient. This blend results in a sauce that is not just spicy, but also richly aromatic and bursting with umami.
The Art of Smashing Chicken

Why smash the chicken? Smashing the chicken after grilling it "opens" the meat, creating small pockets and textures where the sambal sauce can deeply integrate. Each bite delivers a harmonious explosion of flavours, soaked into the meat rather than merely sitting on the surface.
Our Preparation Process

Our cherished house-made Sambal Ulek has been perfected over 30 years. For the Sambal Inasal, we generously brush this sauce onto the freshly smashed chicken. This technique ensures the sauce clings to every fragment of the chicken, enhancing the dish with a silky, enriched flavour profile that redefines the traditional Inasal.
Perfect Pairing

To fully enjoy Bintang's Sambal Inasal, we recommend pairing it with a simple bowl of plain rice. This allows the complex flavours of the sambal sauce to shine, making every spoonful a delightful experience. The rice not only complements the dish but also serves to absorb the abundant sauce, ensuring no drop of flavour is lost.
We invite you to Bintang to experience this culinary innovation - a dish where tradition meets creativity, promising not just a meal, but an unforgettable flavour journey.

image.alt: Glazed, charred chicken inasal on a plate

runs.text: If you're craving a taste of authentic Filipino cuisine, Bintang Restaurant in Camden is the place to go. With their commitment to using high-quality ingredients and cooking methods, Bintang is known for serving up the best Chicken Inasal in London.
What is Chicken Inasal?

Chicken Inasal is a popular Filipino dish that originates from the city of Bacolod in the Visayas region of the Philippines. At Bintang Restaurant, their version of Chicken Inasal is made by marinating the chicken in a mixture of vinegar, calamansi, garlic, ginger, lemongrass, and annatto oil, which gives the chicken its distinctive yellow-orange color and flavor. The chicken is then grilled to perfection over oak wood, adding a smoky flavor that sets it apart from other grilled chicken dishes.
What Makes Bintang's Chicken Inasal the Best in London?

At Bintang, their commitment to using high-quality ingredients and cooking methods sets their Chicken Inasal apart from the rest. By using oak wood in the grilling process, the chicken is infused with a smoky flavor that enhances its taste and texture. Additionally, their unique marinade recipe ensures that every bite of the chicken is packed with flavor. Whether you're a Filipino food lover or a first-timer, Bintang's Chicken Inasal is a must-try.
Filipino FlavoUr Offerings at Bintang Restaurant

While Chicken Inasal is the star of the show at Bintang, their menu also features a range of other classic Filipino dishes that are sure to delight your taste buds. Here are some of the Filipino flavor offerings available at Bintang:
Small Plates

If you're looking for a light snack or appetizer to share, Bintang's Small Plates are the perfect option. These small bites are inspired by Filipino pulutan or bar snacks and include options like Lumpiang Shanghai, Tofu Bites, Chicken Liver Popcorn, and Okoy Fritters.
Large Plates

For a more substantial meal, Bintang's Large Plates offer a variety of Pan Asian and Filipino fusion dishes. In addition to their signature Chicken Inasal, they also offer curries like the Bintang Curry and Ulek Curry (a vegan option), as well as Filipino favorites like Beef Sisig and Pritong Isda.

Bintang Restaurant in Camden is a must-visit for anyone looking to taste authentic Filipino cuisine in London. With their commitment to using high-quality ingredients and cooking methods, their Chicken Inasal is truly the best in London. And with a range of other Filipino flavor offerings available, as well as delivery and takeaway options, there's no reason not to give Bintang a try.

runs.text: Say Goodbye to BYOB and Hello to Filipino-Inspired Cocktails at Bintang Restaurant!

We are excited to announce that we are saying goodbye to our beloved “Bring Your Own Bottle” policy and introducing a brand new menu of Filipino-inspired cocktails and alcohol! Our new menu will feature a range of refreshing and innovative drinks, each with its own unique twist that perfectly embodies the spirit of Filipino hospitality.
Filipino Cocktails
Introducing a brand new array of classic to signature drinks, our new alcohol programme will definitely compliment your dining experience at Bintang

From classic cocktails like the Lychee Daiquiri, inspired by one of the Philippines exciting fruits - Lychee, to new and exciting creations like the Tequila Milk Punch - our menu has something for everyone. Our bartenders have taken the time to craft each drink with care, using only the finest ingredients and a touch of creativity to bring you the best possible experience.
Pandan Old Fashioned

Introducing one of Bintang’s new and signature Pandan Old Fashioned is a type of cocktail that combines traditional Old Fashioned ingredients with the unique flavour of pandan leaves. Pandan is a tropical plant commonly used in Southeast Asian cuisine for its sweet, nutty flavor. In this cocktail, the pandan flavor is typically incorporated through the use of a special pandan-infused simple syrup.

The Pandan Old Fashioned typically contains whiskey, our special pandan-infused simple syrup, and bitters. The ingredients are mixed together and served over ice, typically in a rocks glass. This cocktail offers a unique twist on the classic Old Fashioned, combining the familiar flavors of whiskey and bitters with the sweet and nutty flavor of pandan.

In addition to our new cocktails, we will also be offering a selection of premium beers, wines, and spirits to complement your meal. Whether you're in the mood for a crisp, refreshing beer or a smooth glass of red wine, we have something for you.

posts.title: Good Morning, Silog!
posts.excerpt: Feeling peckish? Don’t feel like the normal breakfast routine? or you simply can’t be bothered to cook something quick in the morning?

image.alt: Bintang’s Breakfast Silog poster: a skillet of egg, rice and sausage drawn on red

runs.text: Rice n’ Shine!
Feeling peckish? Don’t feel like the normal breakfast routine? or you simply can’t be bothered to cook something quick in the morning?
Put your feet up and leave us to cook you one.

The Philippines isn’t just the home to some of the finest beaches in the world but also the craziest breakfast plate on the planet which is called silog. What is Silog? It’s simply two words combined together: which is sinangag (fried rice) and itlog (egg). It isn’t your normal Eggs Ben, but a Filipino take to an All Day Breakfast.
Fancy eating breakfast like Filipinos? We present to you the anatomy of Bintang’s very own silog:
The Foundation Garlic Fried Rice

You might be thinking - that’s nuts! Why would you bloody eat rice for breakfast? But we like to challenge the status quo by having this as the foundation of breakfast. Carbohydrates are good for you - so give your body enough energy it needs to get through your day.

The Brekky Staple Egg Is it really breakfast without this piece of ingredient? The egg is every breakfast’s star - this is your primary source of protein as you start the day. We personally serve this staple to you sunny side up - enough to keep you smiling for the rest of the day.

The Protagonist Your choice of main Like every film or series, there is the lead star - but in this context of silog, we couldn’t keep up with the demand so we give you the liberty to choose your main ulam (viand) with these three superstars:

Tortang Talong If you’re not feeling the meat, our fried aubergine omelette is the perfect combination Longganisa This is a Filipino take to chorizo, we personally make our own by mixing lamb and beef Tapa We cure thin cuts of sirloin beef steak - soft, sweet, and tender!
The Refresher Pickled Salad

Commonly known as the atchara - this is our take on a side dish for this breakfast heavyweight. Our silogs are normally very sweet as a whole, so we like to bring something to refresh your palette as the final ingredients to bring this breakfast into another flavour using carrots, cucumber, and onion.

We like to think that these four combinations present you to a flavoursome firework on a plate. If you definitely want something filling, then this breakfast is definitely for you. If you can’t bring yourself to eat this heavy for breakfast alternatively, you can also order them for your lunch or dinner.

posts.title: 5 Filipino Dishes You’ve Never Heard Of
posts.excerpt: Cuisine in the Philippines varies from region to region and tend to be influenced by the resources and products from that area.

image.alt: A curry, a burger and sesame-crusted bites on a wooden table

runs.text: Cuisine in the Philippines varies from region to region and tend to be influenced by the resources and products from that area. It is interesting to note that food from the Philippines has also been shaped by its deep history of being colonised and occupied by Spain, US, Japan, even China. The migration of the people into Philippines from the neighbouring countries, as well as the rich trading between them, has also moulded the cuisine around the islands.

That’s why you’ll find that the cuisine from Mindanao can be much richer with exotic spices, as delicacies from this southernmost part of the Philippines, are heavily influenced by the surrounding Malay archipelago such as Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. The same way that in the Visaya region which is surrounded by water, the plates from those islands are abundant with seafood. In the north, as they predominantly focus on agriculture, their specialities are in the vegetables they farm but with some more Spanish and Japanese influences. However, in recent years with the rise of OFW’s in the Middle East, there have been many Arab-influenced dishes and chains popping up around, demonstrating the range of the Filipino people’s palette.

As the cuisine from Mindanao receives the least coverage, we thought we’d show them some more love and appreciation with 5 Filipino dishes you may have never heard of. Read the article below to find out more!
The hidden gems in Filipino cuisine
Beef Kulma

A Beef Kulma originates from the Tausug people, a Muslim ethnic group in Mindanao. The dish closely resembles and sounds like a Korma. However, what makes this dish a Mindanao speciality, is that it can be described as being a combination of the Filipino peanut-based Kare-Kare stew and coconut-based beef curry (as referenced by
angsarap
). A fusion of the two creates this spicy peanut beef novelty in Mindanao.
This dish was recently an Eid speciality at Bintang but has been one of our highly requested mains since. Stay tuned on our IG @bintang_restaurant as it might have a permanent place on our menu soon.
Bintang’s Beef Kulma
Filipino Rendang

Rendang is usually known as an Indonesian speciality but the Philippines also have a variant of this dish in Mindanao. A Filipino rendang is a spicy coconut milk beef stew. This dish a lot saucier than the drier Indonesian classic and the method of cooking this rendang is similar to the method of cooking adobo. However, there is no one way to cook an adobo as it too also varies depending on the district, so some may like theirs drier whilst some cook it with a soup-like consistency.
At Bintang: the Filipino rendang is one of our most popular mains, as it is a slow-cooked curried lamb on the bone with coconut and lemongrass, and a little more on the saucier side.
Bintang’s Filipino Lamb Rendang
Satti de Zamboanga
Photo referenced from
Wazzuppilipinas

The Satti resembles a Malaysian and Indonesian satay but is a portion of breakfast food in Zamboanga, Mindanao. It is made of 3 small pieces of meat which are skewered and grilled as is done with bbq. The satti is served with rice balls and a sweet and spicy soup-like sauce, also known as sambal soup. Read more about this Zamboangan speciality on
Wazzuppilipinas
or watch how it is made on the street of the Philippines on
pinoyhowto
below.
Beef Brisket Sisig

Originally the sisig originated from Pampanga in north - central Philippines, as a vinegary salad of pork and papayas seasoned with calamansi. The recipe has been refined and popularised over the years by Lucia "Aling Lucing" Cunanan from Angeles City, Pampanga.

At Bintang: The Beef Brisket Sisig is chopped cured beef brisket, sautéed with chicken liver pate, ginger, chillies and topped with a fresh fried egg to be mixed. Making it a Filipino dish you’ve never technically heard of, so we’ll let this one slide.
Read more about our Beef Brisket Sisig, here.
Bintang’s ever popular, Beef Brisket Sisig
Buko Suka Manok

Literally translating to coconut vinegar chicken, this may not be a traditional Filipino dish in itself but it sure does encompass the palette of the Philippines and especially the island of Mindanao. A Bintang Restaurant original and created by chef owner, Omar Shah. The Buko Suka is fashioned with crispy toyomansi marinated chicken thighs, doused with sea salt & pinakurat (which is a Philippine novelty that is coconut vinegar). As Filipinos, you know how important vinegar is to us! The Buko Suka is also topped off with charred spring onions and sour cream, sundried tomato oil and sumac on roti bread.
Bintang’s Buko Suka
Pinakurat. Photo from
Akabanebusan
Halal Filipino restaurant in London

Mindanao is the southernmost region of the Philippines and has the largest native Muslim population. You’ll find that some of the dishes listed above are not only a speciality of Mindanao but of the native Moro people. The Moro’s ancestors immigrated from the Malay peninsula and Arab countries (read more about the ‘Moro’ people here), hence why you might’ve noticed some similarities from the neighbouring countries.
Read more about Bintang Restaurant on Halal Gems
here

Being the only 100% Filipino Halal restaurant in Europe, at Bintang, we’re celebrating the diversity of Filipino delicacies by bringing them to the table. Our Bintang version of the dishes listed above, as well as the other Philippine-inspired mains and sides we have on our menu, are all halal certified so that everyone can relish in the variety of food from the Philippines and its culture.

posts.title: The ‘Moro’ People of the Philippines
posts.excerpt: The Bangsamoro ‘moro’ people are the native Muslim inhabitants of the Philippines. They are the descendants of the early Malay, Arab and Indian migrants…

image.alt: An archive photograph of three Moro women in traditional dress

runs.text: Short History of the Muslims in the Philippines

The Bangsamoro ‘moro’ people are the native Muslim inhabitants of the Philippines. They are the descendants of the early Malay, Arab and Indian migrants into the Philippine archipelago from as early as the 14th century. The Moro people formed their own ethnic group in southwestern Mindanao, Sulu islands and Palawan. The majority of the Muslims in the Philippines live in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM). Within the Filipino population, there are at least 5 million Muslims across the entire population of the Philippine Islands.

Due to the history of the Islam religion in the Philippines, those in the Muslim community have been known to not to call themselves Filipino Muslims due to King Spain II decreeing ‘the Expulsion of Moriscos’ in 1609, after naming the archipelago after him. The ‘Moro’ name however, was given by the Spanish inquisitors who named the Muslims in the Philippines as such due to their geographical location of living on the moors. This title usually excludes Filipinos who have converted to Islam.
Mindanao Cuisine at Bintang

The Muslims in the Philippines have been disregarded for many years but with the celebration of Eid just a couple of days away - to celebrate with our Muslim brothers and sisters, Bintang have created a Beef Kulma dish based off the Mindanao cuisine. It wouldn’t be right for us to be a Filipino - pan Asian restaurant in London without paying respects to the Muslim people of the Philippines.
Also, all our dishes are halal certified! So make sure to head on over and have a Bintang meal of your own!

runs.text: As a Muslim it can be hard to find somewhere that caters to your needs, especially food wise. Eating halal can be a struggle when looking for somewhere that is not a hot, greasy chicken and chips takeaway shop. I mean yes London is known for it’s PFC’s (Perfect Fried Chicken), Morley’s and Sam’s. However sometimes a lunch that consists of fighting 4ft humans in school uniform inside a cramp 4 x 4 square meter space and leaving with an unfriendly companion that clings to our clothes called chip fat, just doesn’t seems like the best idea.

No need to keep searching “Best halal restaurant” or “Halal restaurants in London”. Bintang gives you a taste of beautiful East Asia, and it’s all permissible. Take your pick from halal Filipino, halal Korean, halal Chinese, halal Thai and halal Japanese cuisines and if you want to try a bit of everything and really pleasure those taste buds, then that is an experience we can definitely give you and food is more than reasonably priced.
